query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Implementing enhanced free energy sampling methods during thermal processing enables more precise control over the phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs by identifying key transformation pathways and critical compositional/thermal thresholds.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA in its as‐cast or solutionized state
generation.intervention: Use advanced free energy sampling techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo or other enhanced sampling strategies) to map the free energy landscape, then tailor annealing and cooling protocols based on the identified transformation pathways.
generation.conditions: Precise thermal processing conditions, including controlled annealing temperatures and cooling rates as determined by the free energy mapping.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution and stabilization of constituent phases (e.g., FCC and BCC) through atomic diffusion and phase transformation kinetics.
generation.mechanism: By quantifying free energy barriers and kinetic pathways, the advanced sampling method guides the selection of specific thermal thresholds that preferentially stabilize desired phases while suppressing others, thereby enabling targeted phase control.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to standard thermal treatments, the HEA will exhibit a phase composition with a higher proportion of the target phase (or a more tailored FCC/BCC ratio), leading to improved compositional and microstructural predictability.
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs undergoing conventional thermal processing, which yield less predictable and less controllable phase evolution.
generation.boundary: The approach’s effectiveness could be limited by the inherent complexity of multi‐principal element systems and uncertainties in simulation predictions under real processing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the method is expected to enhance control over phase evolution, the exact magnitude of improvement in phase selectivity and microstructural retention remains uncertain until validated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples: one undergoing thermal treatments designed based on the free energy sampling insights and one undergoing standard thermal processing. Use X-ray diffraction, scanning/transmission electron microscopy, and mechanical testing to compare phase compositions and properties.
measurements: Phase fractions (e.g., FCC vs BCC ratios) via XRD
Microstructural details (grain size, morphology) via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed with the tailored, free energy sampling–informed thermal protocols do not exhibit a statistically significant and reproducible difference in phase evolution or mechanical properties compared to those processed conventionally, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. frame.goal: To control the phase evolution (i.e., the formation and transformation of constituent phases such as FCC and BCC) during processing in order to tailor microstructure and resulting properties
frame.limitation: The inherent complexity of multi‐principal element alloys makes the evolution of phases less predictable and more sensitive to processing parameters
constraints: method must be applicable to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs
needs to provide a level of control over the phase formation and transformation processes
frame.regime: Thermal processing conditions (e.g., controlled annealing temperatures and cooling rates) that dictate diffusion kinetics and phase stability

families.principle: Advanced sampling techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo or enhanced sampling methods) to map free energy landscapes and kinetic pathways that dictate phase stability and transformation.
families.best_lever: Implementing enhanced free energy sampling methods to identify key transformation pathways and critical compositional/thermal thresholds that can be targeted during annealing.

families.principle: Leveraging data-driven approaches to correlate processing conditions and compositional variables with phase outcomes using statistical or machine learning models.
cues_against: the inherent complexity and multi‐principal element interactions may challenge purely data‐driven predictions without physical insight
families.best_lever: Constructing a machine learning model that, trained on both experimental and simulation data, predicts optimal annealing temperatures and cooling rates for desired phase stability.

families.principle: Atomistic simulations using interatomic potentials to model and predict phase stability and transformation dynamics.
cues_against: control of phase evolution (the question emphasizes tailoring processes rather than only predicting outcomes)
families.best_lever: Refining and tuning interatomic potentials to better capture phase stability differences under processing conditions.

families.principle: In situ experimental techniques (such as synchrotron X‐ray diffraction or high‐resolution electron microscopy) to directly monitor the evolution and kinetics of phase transformations.
cues_against: control of phase evolution (measurement alone does not allow direct control over processing parameters)
families.best_lever: Developing real‐time characterization setups to observe phase changes that could be later coupled with process control, though not directly controlling the phases.
